articles.headline: OFAC Designates Chinese Entities Under Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). These actions target entities involved in activities that undermine American intellectual property.

As part of these designations, OFAC has also issued associated General Licenses to guide compliance and minimize unintended impacts. The specific entities added to OFAC's Non-SDN Menu-Based Sanctions List include BEIJING QIJI CHUANGTAN PHASE I VENTURE CAPITAL CENTER LIMITED PARTNERSHIP (a.k.a. MIRACLE PLUS RMB FUND I).

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-related General License and Issues New FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Venezuela-related General License, alongside a new Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). This update aims to clarify existing sanctions policies and provide guidance for certain transactions involving Venezuela.

The amendment reflects ongoing adjustments to the U.S. sanctions program concerning Venezuela, which has seen some recent shifts in policy. These changes are part of broader efforts to navigate the complex political and economic landscape of the region.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related and Cuba Designations, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting individuals and entities connected to Iran and Cuba. These actions are accompanied by the issuance of new and amended General Licenses, along with updated Frequently Asked Questions.

The Iran-related designations are part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' aiming to restrict the Islamic Republic's access to foreign currency, international banking networks, and oil export revenues. Among the newly sanctioned entities are two offshore banks affiliated with Bank Mellat and Bank Shahr, an Iraqi bank, and a network involved in Iranian oil sales. Cuba's Banco Internacional de Comercio S.A. (BICSA) was also targeted due to its ties to Iran.

These measures underscore the U.S. government's continued pressure on both Iran and Cuba, with a focus on disrupting financial networks and illicit activities. The new General Licenses and FAQs are intended to provide clarity for legitimate transactions while maintaining the integrity of the sanctions programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuelan National Assembly President Jorge Rodriguez from Sanctions List
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has officially removed Jorge Rodriguez, the president of Venezuela's National Assembly, from its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) blacklist. This action signals a potential shift in U.S. policy towards Venezuela.

Rodriguez, who has led the Venezuelan parliament since 2021, was initially designated in September 2018. His delisting follows a period of increased political and economic engagement between Washington and Caracas, particularly after the ouster of former President Nicolas Maduro in January.

The removal of sanctions on Rodriguez comes months after similar actions were taken against his sister, Delcy Rodriguez, and amid reports of major U.S.-Venezuela energy pacts. This move is seen as part of a broader effort by the Trump administration to open up Venezuela's energy industry to American companies.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Al Jazeera / Reuters

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to disrupt illicit networks that pose threats to U.S. national security.

These designations aim to sever financial and material support for criminal organizations and terrorist groups globally. The U.S. government continues to utilize its sanctions authorities to combat these pervasive threats.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued a new General License related to Russia. This license provides specific authorizations for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under existing Russia sanctions programs.

The issuance of General Licenses often indicates a refinement of sanctions policy, aiming to facilitate humanitarian aid, certain commercial activities, or other specific objectives while maintaining overall pressure on the sanctioned regime.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Iran-related Designations and Amends Russia-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations and issued an associated Iran-related General License. Concurrently, OFAC has also issued an amended Russia-related General License.

The Iran-related actions are part of the ongoing 'Operation Economic Outcast,' which targets Iran's shadow fleet network and aims to disrupt its illicit oil trade and financial lifelines. These measures are designed to increase pressure on the Iranian regime by severing its access to international financial systems.

The amended Russia-related General License indicates further adjustments to the U.S. sanctions framework concerning Russia, likely to address evolving geopolitical and economic considerations. These dual actions highlight the dynamic nature of U.S. sanctions policy in response to global challenges.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Designations Removals, Updates, and Iran-related Alert
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced several designations removals and updates, alongside the publication of an Iran-related OFAC Alert and an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). These actions reflect ongoing adjustments to sanctions lists and guidance.

The OFAC Alert specifically warns foreign financial institutions about the risks of doing business with Iran or its financial sector, emphasizing that they may be sanctioned under 'Operation Economic Outcast' without prior notification. This alert reinforces the U.S. government's commitment to disrupting Iran's access to the global financial system.

The designations removals and updates indicate a continuous review of sanctions targets, while the amended FAQ provides further clarification on existing Iran-related sanctions. These measures aim to enhance the effectiveness and precision of the sanctions program.

articles.headline: EU Adopts Largest-Ever Sanctions Package Against Russia's Military-Industrial Complex
body: The Council of the European Union has adopted its largest-ever package of restrictive measures against Russia, targeting 1,569 individuals and entities within Russia's military and industrial complex. This action follows calls from the European Council in June 2026 to escalate pressure on Russia in response to its ongoing aggression against Ukraine.

The new listings include 826 Russian companies and 743 CEOs, bringing the total number of designations under the Russia sanctions regime to almost 4,600. These sanctions primarily target mid-level suppliers that form the core of Russia's military industry, generating significant annual turnover and employing a large workforce.

The measures impose an asset freeze on those listed and prohibit the provision of funds or economic resources to them. Additionally, a travel ban to the EU applies to the natural persons designated. The EU emphasizes that these actions aim to constrain Russia's industrial capacity, particularly concerning components used in missiles, UAVs, and aircraft.
articles.source: Council of the EU / Hill Dickinson / Morgan Lewis

articles.headline: EU Sanctions Individuals and Entities for DPRK Nuclear and Missile Programs, Russia Ties
body: The Council of the European Union has adopted additional restrictive measures against three individuals and four entities under its autonomous sanctions list on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK). These designations are in response to their support for DPRK's nuclear weapons, ballistic missile programs, and evasion of United Nations sanctions.

The new listings specifically target activities linked to the growing military and economic cooperation between the DPRK and Russia, including the deployment of DPRK workers in Russia, commercial and industrial cooperation, and an 'arms-for-oil' trade, all in violation of UN Security Council prohibitions.

Among the sanctioned entities are Russian real estate developer Samolet Group and its CEO, Anna Nikolaevna Akinshina, for employing North Korean workers, and Vladimir Aleksandrovich Sokolov, founder of Black Horse, for facilitating commercial cooperation. Paekyangsan Shipping Co Ltd and Golden Autumn Agroholding were also listed for their involvement in illicit shipments and industrial investment projects.
articles.source: Council of the EU / The Brussels Times

articles.headline: President Trump Waives New Russia Sanctions Under Graham Act Amid Deteriorating Ukraine Relations
body: President Donald Trump has issued an executive order waiving new sanctions and tariffs on Russia, which were passed by Congress in the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. This move comes just days before the sanctions were set to take effect and amid a deepening rift between the Trump administration and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

The legislation, championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, aimed to more quickly curb the flow of financial resources fueling Russia's war against Ukraine. It included sanctions on Russian officials, banks, and a 'shadow fleet' of tankers transporting Russian energy, as well as directives for tariffs on top importers of Russian oil or natural gas.

Trump's decision to pause these sanctions has been met with criticism from some members of Congress, who view it as a betrayal of Ukraine and the will of the legislature. The President has publicly criticized Ukraine for its attacks on Russian oil refineries, which he blames for contributing to global diesel shortages, and has suggested that Ukraine needs a new leader.
articles.source: Reuters / The Guardian / Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Settles with OFAC for $11,662,930

The specific details of the violations leading to this substantial penalty have been outlined in the settlement agreement. Financial institutions are expected to maintain robust compliance programs to prevent breaches of U.S. sanctions regulations.

The resolution of this case highlights OFAC's continued enforcement efforts against companies that fail to comply with U.S. sanctions. Businesses involved in international logistics are particularly vulnerable to sanctions risks and are expected to implement effective compliance measures.

articles.headline: Global Diesel Shortage Reshapes U.S. Foreign Policy, Fuels Debate on Russian Imports
body: Record-high global diesel prices are significantly influencing U.S. foreign policy, particularly concerning Russia and Ukraine. The Trump administration's decision to waive new sanctions on Russia and consider purchasing Russian diesel has sparked considerable debate and criticism.

President Trump has attributed the global diesel shortage, in part, to Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries, while Ukraine maintains these refineries are crucial to Russia's war funding. This divergence in perspective has led to a dramatic deterioration in relations between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

The move to potentially import Russian diesel, a reversal of years of U.S. and Western pressure on the Kremlin, is aimed at bringing down domestic fuel prices ahead of the American midterm elections. Critics argue this decision betrays Ukraine and funds Russia's war efforts.

articles.headline: Houthi Rebels Strike Yemeni Government Forces, Killing Dozens
body: Iran-backed Houthi rebels have launched a ballistic missile attack on a Yemeni government military camp, resulting in the deaths of at least 53 soldiers. The strike marks a significant escalation in the ongoing conflict in Yemen.

The attack underscores the persistent instability and violence in the region, with various factions continuing to engage in hostilities. International efforts to de-escalate the conflict and find a peaceful resolution have faced considerable challenges.

articles.headline: France Experiences Worst Civil Unrest in Years as Rioters Clash with Police
body: France has been gripped by its worst civil unrest in years, with rioters clashing violently with police, setting vehicles ablaze, and storming public buildings. A historic city hall was engulfed in flames during the widespread disturbances.
The unrest highlights deep-seated social and political tensions within the country. Authorities are working to restore order and address the underlying causes of the widespread protests and violence.

articles.headline: Homeland Security Grants Temporary Deportation Reprieve for Ukrainians and Sudanese
body: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has granted a temporary deportation reprieve for over 100,000 individuals from Ukraine and Sudan residing in the U.S. Their Temporary Protected Status (TPS) was set to expire, but DHS has announced they will retain protection until a further announcement is made.

This decision provides a temporary extension of legal status for these populations, allowing them to remain in the United States without fear of deportation. The measure addresses humanitarian concerns stemming from ongoing conflicts and instability in their home countries.

articles.headline: Kenyan Cult Pastor Paul Mackenzie Faces Judgment in Mass Murder Case
body: A Kenyan judge has begun delivering a verdict in the mass murder case involving doomsday preacher Paul Mackenzie. Mackenzie and 29 of his followers are charged with the murder of 191 people, predominantly children, who are alleged to have been forced to starve to death to 'meet Jesus'.

Mackenzie and his co-defendants have pleaded not guilty to the murder charges, consistently asserting that no one was forced to die. The trial has drawn significant international attention due to the horrific nature of the allegations and the large number of victims.

The judgment in this high-profile case is expected to have profound implications for religious cults and accountability for such atrocities in Kenya and beyond. The proceedings continue to unfold as the court determines the fate of those accused.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
